extracted.intended_audience: authors of mathematical research papers, especially non-native English speakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and phrase-bank for composing clear, idiomatic mathematical research papers in English, covering abstracts, introductions, definitions, theorems, proofs, notation, grammar, and editorial correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract and introduction: state main results and aims concisely
rubrics_metrics.description: State what is proved or shown, indicate scope and applications, and make the purpose explicit (e.g. “We prove that …”, “Our purpose is to …”, “The aim of this paper is to …”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct sentences such as “We prove that …”, “It is of interest to know whether …”, “Our theorem provides a natural and intrinsic characterization of ….”; avoid vague or empty openings. Indicate whether proofs appear here or elsewhere (e.g. “The detailed proofs will appear in …”, “For the proofs we refer the reader to …”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract/introduction: outline paper structure and section content
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefly indicate what each section contains and what the paper will do (e.g. “In the third section we review …”, “Section 4 contains …”, “The remainder of this section will be devoted to …”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise phrases: “In the third section …”, “Section 4 is devoted to the study of …”, “The remainder of this section will be devoted to the proof of …”. Note: paragraph ≠ section; be specific about what is summarized, sketched, or proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid empty or tautological introductory sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use sentences that convey no information (e.g. “We now have the following lemma”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove sentences that merely announce a statement without content; prefer direct formulations of results or brief useful signposting only when it adds information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: standard concise formulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Give clear definition patterns such as “A set S is dense if …”, “We call a set dense if …”, “By the length of T we mean …”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conventional constructions (“is called”, “is defined by”, “we say that”) and watch word order after phrases like “we call”. Use infinitives appropriately when introducing definitions (e.g. “This map is defined by requiring f to be constant on …”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation: introduce and abbreviate consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce notation explicitly (e.g. “Let us denote by Z …”, “We will denote by clA the closure of A”, “For simplicity of notation …”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid careless uses such as “Denote f = …”. Use remarks like “For brevity/for short/for simplicity” sparingly and do not use incorrect phrases (“in short”, “shortly”). Prefer “We write …” or “We will write … when no confusion can arise.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Print/typography terminology and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use consistent terminology for typefaces and symbols (e.g. italics, bold print, parentheses, square brackets, braces, capitals vs small letters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit when necessary: e.g. “The expression in italics, in large type, in bold print; in parentheses ( ) (= round brackets), in brackets [ ] (= square brackets), in braces { } (= curly brackets) …” Use agreed notation for special alphabets (Gothic, script, blackboard bold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property phrasing: use correct connectors and avoid awkward constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrase properties using conventional patterns: “such that”, “with the property that”, “satisfying …”, “depending only on …”, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid incorrect forms like “such an element that”. Use constructions like “so small that …”, “may be made arbitrarily small by …”, and ensure negatives and coordinations use correct word order (“not continuous, nor do they satisfy …”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions/conditions/conventions: explicit and economical
rubrics_metrics.description: State standing assumptions clearly (e.g. “We will make the following assumptions: …”, “Unless otherwise stated we assume that …”, “Without loss of generality we can assume …”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use infinitive constructions where appropriate (“requiring g to be …”, “imposing the condition: …”). If an assumption is not restrictive, say so (e.g. “This condition is not particularly restrictive”). Indicate when you tacitly adopt a convention (e.g. “We adopt the convention that 0/0 = 0”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem statements: clear hypotheses and conclusions; avoid redundant phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate theorems in conditional patterns (e.g. “If … and if …, then …”, “Let M be … Assume that … Then …”), give equivalent conditions explicitly, and avoid unnecessary repetition of assumptions already stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise markers like “Under the above assumptions …”, “The following conditions are equivalent: …”, and drop filler expressions such as “the following inequality holds” unless informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem introductory phrases: use informative lead-ins
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce consequences, analogues, or specializations with concise lead-ins (e.g. “We have thus proved …”, “Summarizing, we have …”, “We are thus led to …”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid purely rhetorical lead-ins that add no information. Indicate when a result strengthens or specializes another (“This is a strengthening of Theorem 6”, “This specializes to the result of [7] if …”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof: beginning—explicit strategy and first steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Start proofs with a clear plan (e.g. “We first prove that …”, “To this end, consider …”, “The proof consists in the construction of …”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use idiomatic English: prefer “For this purpose” instead of “To this aim”. State if proof is by induction, contradiction, or split into steps; avoid leaving the method implicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof: arguments—use correct logical connectors and avoid incorrect constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use correct connective phrases (“Hence”, “It follows that”, “By Theorem 4 we have …”) and avoid wrong patterns like “Since …, then …”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State derivations clearly: prefer “It follows that Lf = 0” or “Therefore Lf = 0 by Theorem 6”. Use explicit reasons when needed (“because …”, “for otherwise …”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof: consecutive steps—imperative, let/set, and ing-forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize stepwise operations with verbs like “Let”, “Set”, or gerund phrases used correctly (e.g. “Adding g to the left-hand side”, “Combining (3) with (6)”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the imperative mood implication: don’t use an imperative when you mean to describe what you did. Use ing-forms either as subjects (“Adding … gives …”) or with explicit subject (“Adding … we obtain …”), but not wrongly (“Adding … the proof is complete” is incorrect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof: use of 'It suffices to …' phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use succinct reductions: “It suffices to show that …”, “We only need to consider three cases …”, “The statement will be proved once we prove …”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase reductions cleanly and list remaining tasks clearly. Use this to structure proofs by reduction to simpler claims or lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof: 'It is easily seen that …' and similar phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark straightforward or routine verifications with phrases like “It is clear that …”, “It is easily seen that …”, “A trivial verification shows that …”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these phrases sparingly and where the omitted details are genuinely routine; avoid overusing them to hide nontrivial steps. Examples: “It follows easily that …”, “Of course, …”.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof: conclusion and remarks—explicitly close and indicate consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: End proofs with clear concluding sentences (“This proves the theorem”, “The proof is complete”), indicate corollaries or further consequences and note limitations of the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concluding phrases like “We leave it to the reader to verify …” when appropriate; indicate if a proof gives more than the stated result (“Note that we have actually proved that …”). Avoid incorrect nouns like “thesis” for theorem conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: References to literature: concise citation phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to previous work with concise cross-references (e.g. “see [7]”, “for a deeper discussion see [7]”, “This was proved by Lax [8]”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent citation forms (“see [Ka2] for …”, “we follow [Ka] in assuming …”). When summarizing earlier results, be clear if something is adapted, motivated by, or generalizes prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgments: standard phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge help and support using conventional expressions (“The author wishes to express his thanks to …”, “The author gratefully acknowledges …”, “This is part of the author’s Ph.D. thesis …”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention institutions providing hospitality or financial support and collaborators’ contributions with concise customary phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to shorten the paper: write for experts and remove redundancies
rubrics_metrics.description: General rules: write for an expert, cross out trivial/routine material, avoid repetition of assumptions and conclusions, and check necessity of each formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific advice: remove phrases like “We denote by R the set …”, shorten common phrases (e.g. “Let ε be an arbitrary but fixed positive number” → “Fix ε > 0”), use equation labels instead of repeating formulas, and replace long phrases with concise equivalents (see examples on p.20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial correspondence: submission and revision phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard polite forms when communicating with editors (e.g. “I would like to submit the enclosed manuscript …”, “Please find enclosed two copies of the revised version”, “I regret any inconvenience this may have caused you”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State actions clearly (submit, withdraw, revise), mention changes made per referee suggestions, and include required materials (reprints, copies) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee’s report: conventional evaluative language
rubrics_metrics.description: Sample referee phrases range from positive recommendation to rejection (e.g. “The author proves the interesting result that …”, “I strongly recommend it for publication”, “Accordingly, I recommend that the paper be rejected”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific critical comments (e.g. “condition B should be formulated more carefully”), indicate correctness, originality, significance and English quality, and list minor typographical errors when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite article (a, an, —): usage rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use “a/an” according to pronunciation; use indefinite article for meaning “one of”, “some”, or “a member of a class” and omit when appropriate in plural or class contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “A chapter will be devoted to …”, “A fundamental solution is a function satisfying …”, avoid using article where not required (“In the plural: The elements of D are often called …”). Use ‘a’ or ‘an’ according to sound (e.g. “a unit”, “an x”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definite article (the): usage rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use “the” for uniquely determined objects or when referring back to something mentioned earlier (e.g. “The real measures form a subclass …”, “Let f be the linear form … defined by (2)”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the definite article to objects defined previously or uniquely identified by context; follow examples in the guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article omission: where to omit articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on when no article is needed (e.g. in headings, some mathematical phrases, or plurals referring to general classes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow examples provided (see Part B) and prefer omission where English usage does not require an article; consult specific cases in the document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitive vs ing-form: correct usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the infinitive appropriately (e.g. “To this end”, “To do this, take …”, “requiring f to be constant”) and use gerund (-ing) as subject or with explicit subject only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid incorrect phrases like “To this aim”; use “To this end”. Keep the infinitive for purpose clauses and the -ing form for nominalized actions with clear subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive voice: appropriate and measured use
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive constructions are common in mathematics; use them when the agent is unimportant (“This is proved by …”, “It is shown that …”), but do not overuse to the point of obscuring responsibility or clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance passive and active voice for clarity; prefer active when naming authors or agents is informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiers and determiners: correct selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quantifiers precisely (“every”, “each”, “some”, “any”, “all”, “none”), and follow recommended patterns in mathematical contexts (e.g. “For every point p ∈ M …”, “For all x” as alternative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See examples throughout Part B for use in plural vs singular contexts and for constructions like “There exists … such that …”.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number, quantity and size: plural/singular and comparative uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use grammatical number correctly (“Both X and Y are finite”, “Neither X nor Y is finite”, “There is only one such series for each y”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to constructs like “neither” (refers to two alternatives), “none” and “none of the functions Fi is finite”, and correct comparative forms (“greater than or equal to”).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to avoid repetition: concise rewriting and pronoun use
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid restating assumptions or conclusions unnecessarily; use labels and references instead of repeating formulas or long phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delete trivial repetition (e.g. redundant statements of hypotheses in proofs), replace repeated formulas with labels (equation numbers), and prefer compact expressions (examples provided on p.20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Word order and adverb placement: follow English norms
rubrics_metrics.description: General order: subject + verb + object + adverbs (manner-place-time). Place frequency adverbs between subject and verb; place adverbs referring to the whole sentence at the beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow subrules for adverb positions, inversion in negative or emphatic constructions (e.g. “Only for x = 1 does the limit exist”), and special placements (adverbs between auxiliaries and main verb in compound tenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma insertion: when required, optional, or not needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overuse commas; avoid commas around defining clauses, but use commas for non-defining clauses and where omission causes ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comma not required in many mathematical constructions (“We shall now prove that f is proper.”); comma required in appositives or after introductory phrases (“In this section, however, …”); comma optional in some cases (“By Theorem 2, there exists an h such that …”). Use commas to avoid ambiguity between symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation: consistent forms and required hyphens
rubrics_metrics.description: Use consistent hyphenation conventions (nontrivial vs non-trivial), include hyphen in fixed compounds (“one-parameter group”, “n-fold integration”), and accept optional hyphens in some phrases (“right-hand side” vs “right hand side”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow listed rules: either consistently prefer unhyphenated or hyphenated forms for non-; require hyphenation in certain multiword modifiers; be consistent in the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some typical errors: spelling, grammar, wrong word/word order
rubrics_metrics.description: Common pitfalls include British vs American spelling consistency, incorrect tense with dates, wrong prepositions/phrases (e.g. “disjoint with” vs “disjoint from”), and wrong word-order errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the list of examples (p.46–48) and correct patterns (e.g. “Let f denote” not “Let f denotes”, “Since f = 0, it follows that M is closed”, “We denote this map by f” not “This map we denote by f”).
